newsitem.title: USA: U.S. astronauts get time off.
newsitem.headline: U.S. astronauts get time off.

text.p: Astronauts aboard the space shuttle Columbia, disappointed by the cancellation of their space walks, planned to take time off to relax on Sunday, NASA officials said.
The crew of five were mostly silent overnight after hearing that the two space walks planned for their mission had been cancelled because of Columbia's stuck outer hatch.

NASA engineers were unable to determine why the hatch, leading from the airlock chamber to the cargo bay, had jammed, officials had said on Saturday. They feared attempts to force the door open would only make matters worse and called off two space walks aimed at practicing space station assembly.
The astronauts were given an extra hour of sleep and were scheduled to awake at about 6 p.m. EST (2300 GMT) on Sunday to begin their 13th day in space.

The crew planned to get a six-hour break from work on Sunday evening to take in the view of Earth from 220 miles (352 km) up. Later in the day, they will make private phone calls to family and friends.

NASA managers were considering extending the flight by one day so a U.S.-German orbiting observatory, released from the shuttle on Nov. 19, could make further observations, said mission commentator Kari Fluegel.

The Orfeus-Spas telescope, which was trailing Columbia by about 26 miles (42 km), was due to be plucked from orbit by the shuttle crew on Tuesday morning. The space telescope was studying interstellar matter in an effort to learn more about the life cycles of the stars.

In the original flight plan, Columbia was due to return to Earth on Thursday with a landing at its home base in Florida. Mission managers will decide on Monday whether to extend the flight based on the weather outlook for landing.
